blocks.text: 1. Why Chunking?

blocks.alt: A whole document goes through chunking to produce chunks

blocks.text: Why Chunking opens the Chunking module by explaining why documents get split at all, shifting focus from preparing documents to preparing them for retrieval.
It breaks large, ingested documents into smaller, retrievable pieces.
2. Document Ingestion Recap
The eleven topics in the Document Ingestion module produced clean, normalized, deduplicated documents ready for the next step.
Chunking takes those complete documents and splits them.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Module","Role"],"rows":[["Document Ingestion","Produces clean, complete documents"],["Chunking","Splits those documents into retrievable pieces"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Whole Documents Are Too Big

blocks.alt: A long document is compared against a limited context window

blocks.text: Embedding models accept only a limited amount of text at once.
As covered under context window in Deep Learning Fundamentals, an entire document often exceeds that limit.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Feeding an entire long document into an embedding model at once either fails outright once the limit is exceeded, or gets silently truncated, losing everything past the cutoff.

blocks.text: 4. Retrieval Precision

blocks.alt: A whole document retrieved is compared against a precise relevant chunk

blocks.text: A huge document embedded as a single vector blends many unrelated ideas together.
A smaller, focused chunk produces a sharper, more precise embedding.
5. Chunking As The Bridge

blocks.alt: Raw documents go through chunking to produce indexable units

blocks.text: Chunking sits between Document Ingestion and Embeddings, covered later.
It turns whole documents into retrievable units.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pipeline stage","Input and output"],"rows":[["Document Ingestion","Raw sources in, clean documents out"],["Chunking","Clean documents in, retrievable pieces out"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Tradeoff Of Chunk Size And Context

blocks.alt: A small precise chunk is compared against a large chunk with more context

blocks.text: Chunks that are too small lose surrounding context; chunks that are too large blend unrelated ideas.
Finding the right size is a central tension explored across this entire module.
7. Many Ways To Split

blocks.alt: Fixed, semantic, and recursive are options for splitting

blocks.text: Fixed, recursive, semantic, and sentence based splitting are all different chunking strategies.
Each gets its own dedicated topic later in this module.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: No single chunking strategy works best for every kind of document. This module covers several distinct strategies precisely because the right choice depends on the content being split.

blocks.text: 8. Chunking Quality Shapes Retrieval
Poor chunking produces poor retrieval, no matter how good the embedding model is.
As covered under retrieval using embeddings in What Is RAG, chunking quality limits everything downstream.
9. Recognizing Why Chunking Cannot Be Skipped

blocks.alt: Documents longer than the context window point toward chunking

blocks.text: Any document longer than a single embedding call's limit must be chunked.
Already short, focused documents, by contrast, may need only minimal or no splitting.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates the retrieval precision problem that motivates chunking.

code.content:
long_document = """
Section 1: Company history spans three decades of growth.
Section 2: Product features include analytics and reporting.
Section 3: Refund policy allows returns within thirty days.
Section 4: Contact support through email or live chat.
"""

def fake_embed(text):
    # a real embedding averages meaning across all the text it is given
    words = text.lower().split()
    return {"word_count": len(words), "topics_blended": text.count("Section")}

whole_doc_embedding = fake_embed(long_document)
print("Embedding the whole document at once:")
print(f"  {whole_doc_embedding}")
print("  This single vector blends all four unrelated sections together.\n")

chunks = [line.strip() for line in long_document.strip().split("\n")]
print("Embedding each chunk separately instead:")
for chunk in chunks:
    embedding = fake_embed(chunk)
    print(f"  '{chunk[:40]}...' -> {embedding}")
print("  Each vector now represents one focused idea instead of four blended ones.")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the same document producing one blended, unfocused representation when embedded whole, versus four sharp, topic specific representations when split into chunks first.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Embedding entire long documents as a single vector and wondering why retrieval feels imprecise.
Assuming one chunking strategy works equally well for every kind of document.
Ignoring the embedding model's input length limit until a document silently gets truncated.
Treating chunking as a minor implementation detail rather than a decision that shapes retrieval quality.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Chunking breaks large, ingested documents into smaller, retrievable pieces.
Document Ingestion produces clean documents; chunking splits them for the next stage.
Embedding models accept only a limited amount of text, and whole documents often exceed it.
Smaller, focused chunks produce sharper, more precise embeddings than whole documents.
Chunking bridges Document Ingestion and the upcoming Embeddings module.
Chunks that are too small lose context; chunks that are too large blend unrelated ideas.
Different chunking strategies suit different kinds of content, covered across this module.
Chunking quality places a ceiling on everything retrieval can achieve downstream.
Next up: Fixed Chunking, covering the simplest way to split text into equal sized pieces.
